faq.a: No, it is a benign tumour; malignant transformation does not occur.
faq.q: Can a hepatic hemangioma become cancerous?

faq.a: Rarely; biopsy risks bleeding and is avoided when imaging is characteristic.
Estrogen can enlarge them; switching to non‑estrogen methods is advised if the lesion is large or symptomatic.

ai.title: Hepatic Hemangioma
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Benign vascular liver tumour, usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. Diagnosis relies on imaging; management is conservative unless complications arise.

b: Most patients are asymptomatic; large lesions may cause pain or fullness.
sections.p: Hepatic hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumour, composed of dilated blood‑filled vascular channels. It is found in 0.4‑7 % of imaging studies, often in women of reproductive age.

b: Differential includes focal nodular hyperplasia, hepatic adenoma, metastasis, cyst.
Complications: rupture, Kasabach‑Merritt‑like coagulopathy, compression of biliary tree.
sections.p: Think of a vascular lesion when a liver mass is well‑circumscribed, hyperechoic on ultrasound and shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill‑in on contrast imaging.

b: Rapid growth, pain, or >10 cm size → consider surgery or embolisation.
Pregnancy or oral contraceptive use may enlarge the lesion.
sections.p: Most hemangiomas need no treatment, but clinicians must recognise red‑flag features that prompt further work‑up or intervention.

t.b: Is the lesion cystic or solid? – Shows well‑defined, hyperechoic, homogenous mass; helps rule out solid tumours.
What is the vascular pattern? – Peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill‑in confirms hemangioma; if unavailable, rely on US features and clinical stability.
Is there a malignant liver tumour? – Normal AFP supports benign lesion; elevated AFP suggests hepatocellular carcinoma.

b: Observation with periodic US (6‑12 mo) for small, asymptomatic lesions.
Surgical resection (enucleation) for giant or symptomatic lesions when operative facilities exist.
Trans‑arterial embolisation if surgery not feasible or urgent bleeding.
Avoid estrogen‑containing contraceptives; switch to progestin‑only or barrier methods.
sections.p: Treat only if symptomatic, large, or complicated. Options depend on resources.

b: Focal nodular hyperplasia – central scar, arterial enhancement.
Hepatic adenoma – associated with oral contraceptives, risk of rupture, lacks peripheral nodular pattern.
Metastasis – multiple lesions, irregular borders, rapid growth.
sections.p: Other liver masses can mimic hemangioma on imaging.

b: Small hemangiomas may appear cystic on US, leading to missed diagnosis.
Elevated liver enzymes are usually absent; if present, look for co‑existing disease.
sections.p: Imaging pitfalls and lab values may be misleading.

b: Remember the classic CT/MRI enhancement pattern.
Know when observation is sufficient versus when to refer for surgery.
Consider pregnancy‑related growth as a trigger for re‑evaluation.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, red‑flag identification, and resource‑appropriate decision making.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain suggesting rupture
Rapid increase in lesion size on serial imaging
Signs of consumptive coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen)
